analysis.one_liner: Requires hotels and booking sites to show the full price of a room, including mandatory fees, up front.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Commerce Committee on August 1, 2024 and was placed on the Senate calendar, but never received a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Hotels and booking websites often advertise a low room rate, then add mandatory resort, cleaning, or destination fees at checkout. This bill would have made it illegal to advertise or display a lodging price without also showing the total price including all mandatory fees, with the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general able to enforce it. A committee amendment changed the bill: it excluded government-imposed taxes and fees from the required upfront total, protected booking platforms that rely in good faith on hotels' price information, and barred states from keeping their own stronger advertising rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Travelers booking hotels, motels, and short-term rentals. Anyone comparison-shopping rooms online would see the true total price, including mandatory fees, at the moment the price is first shown, instead of discovering resort or cleaning fees at checkout. This makes real price comparison possible across hotels and booking sites.

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered entities — hotels, short-term rentals, third-party online sellers, and intermediaries like metasearch sites — to clearly and prominently display the total services price wherever lodging is advertised, and to disclose that price when a buyer first sees it and throughout the purchase process.
Requires disclosure, before final purchase, of any tax, fee, or assessment imposed by a government entity or government-created special district on the sale.
Gives the FTC enforcement power as an unfair or deceptive practice, and lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of their residents.
Covers prices shown through direct offerings, third-party distribution, and metasearch referrals, so the rule follows the price wherever a traveler sees it.

analysis.who_pays: Hotels, short-term rental hosts, and online booking platforms, which would have to rework advertising and price-display systems and give up the ability to lure shoppers with low base rates that look cheaper than they are. The bill's compliance deadline was 450 days after enactment.

drawbacks.text: The committee amendment preempts state law: a state or city could no longer maintain or enforce its own rules on advertising lodging prices that exclude mandatory fees, so states with stronger junk-fee bans — or states wanting tougher rules than the federal standard — would be barred from enforcing them.

The required upfront total excludes taxes and fees imposed by governments or government-created districts; those only have to be disclosed before final purchase, so the advertised price still understates the true bottom line in high-tax destinations.

The amendment gives booking intermediaries and third-party online sellers a rebuttable presumption of compliance if they relied in good faith on a hotel's inaccurate price information and corrected it after notice, weakening the threat of liability against the platforms where most travelers shop.
An honest supporter would also note that honest hotels and platforms bear real compliance costs, and that price-display rules require ongoing FTC attention to work as intended.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and everyday: travelers could compare true prices across hotels and booking sites instead of being baited with base rates. The costs are modest compliance burdens on the lodging industry. The bigger tradeoff is in the committee version of the bill: it sets a federal floor but also a ceiling, precluding states from enforcing stronger transparency rules, and it carves government-imposed fees out of the upfront total. On balance the bill would still help travelers, but the amendment made it weaker than the version introduced in 2023, which would have required all mandatory fees in the advertised price.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill favorably and placed it on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but Senate leadership never brought it to the floor for a vote, and the Congress ended with it still waiting.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill in July 2023 with a bipartisan group of cosponsors: Republicans Jerry Moran and Shelley Moore Capito and Democrats Catherine Cortez Masto and Robert Casey.
The original version prohibited advertising or displaying a lodging price that did not include all mandatory fees, with FTC and state attorney general enforcement.

The bill sat in the Commerce Committee for about a year before the committee ordered it reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on July 31, 2024, and it was reported to the Senate on August 1, 2024.

The substitute amendment replaced the flat fee-inclusion ban with a total-price display requirement that excludes government-imposed taxes and fees, and added a preemption section barring states from enforcing their own lodging price-advertising rules and a rebuttable presumption of compliance for online intermediaries.
The reported bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 478, meaning it was awaiting floor time.
No floor vote ever occurred, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lodging operators and online booking platforms kept the status quo: they can still advertise low base rates and add mandatory fees at checkout, and no federal or preempting federal-state rule now applies. Travelers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited bipartisan cosponsors.

for.name: Sens. Jerry Moran, Shelley Moore Capito, Catherine Cortez Masto, Robert Casey
for.role: Original cosponsors (2 of 49 Senate Republicans, 2 of 48 Senate Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing from introduction.

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on August 1, 2024, moving it to the Senate calendar.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote after it was placed on the Senate calendar in August 2024.

against.name: Lodging and online travel booking industry
against.role: Hotels, short-term rental platforms, and online travel agencies
against.what_they_did: Lobbied for a single federal price-display standard with preemption of state rules rather than a patchwork of state junk-fee laws; the committee amendment's preemption, safe-harbor, and government-fee carve-out provisions tracked those preferences.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from introduction, with two of 49 Senate Republicans and two of 48 Senate Democrats cosponsoring, and the Democratic-led Commerce Committee reported it favorably; the opposition was not a party bloc but the absence of floor time.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the practice of advertising low base rates and adding mandatory resort or cleaning fees at checkout, forcing operators to show the true total first. Their interest in keeping headline prices artificially low runs directly against travelers' ability to comparison-shop.

industries.industry: Online travel agencies and metasearch platforms
industries.note: Booking sites and price-comparison platforms would have had to display total prices across their listings, but the committee amendment gave them a safe harbor when relying on hotels' price information and preempted stricter state rules. Their profit from showing low base rates runs against the shopper's interest in seeing the real total.

industries.industry: State attorneys general and state regulators
industries.note: The bill's preemption clause would have stripped states and cities of the power to enforce their own lodging price-advertising rules, even stronger ones, concentrating enforcement in the FTC.
